# Almost Periodicity in Morphic Sequences

This paper establishes precise criteria for determining when certain morphic sequences are almost periodic, a property that is equivalent to the notion of uniform recurrence. A sequence is uniformly recurrent when every factor that appears in it recurs with bounded gaps, meaning that any given pattern reappears within intervals of a predictable maximum length. Understanding when this property holds is a fundamental question in the study of infinite sequences generated by morphisms.

The analysis presented in this work focuses on two specific and important classes of sequences. The first class consists of the fixed points of non-erasing morphisms, which are sequences that remain invariant under the repeated application of a morphism that never maps a symbol to the empty word. The second class comprises automatic sequences, which are sequences whose terms can be computed by a finite automaton reading the digital representation of each position. These two cases represent central objects of study in combinatorics on words and the theory of formal languages.

For both of these classes, the authors present a polynomial-time algorithm that solves the almost periodicity problem. This result is significant because it demonstrates that the property of almost periodicity can be decided efficiently, rather than merely being decidable in principle. The existence of such algorithms provides a practical means of testing uniform recurrence for these well-defined families of sequences.

Beyond their immediate applicability to these specific cases, these findings contribute to a broader theoretical goal. The work provides evidence that lends support to the conjecture that the general decidability problem can be solved. By resolving the question for these important subclasses, the paper strengthens the case that a comprehensive solution to the almost periodicity problem for morphic sequences in general may ultimately be attainable.

# Almost Periodicity of Morphic Sequences

## Introduction

The study of infinite sequences over finite alphabets occupies a central place in combinatorics on words, symbolic dynamics, and theoretical computer science. Among the many structural properties that such sequences may possess, *almost periodicity*—also known as *uniform recurrence*—stands out as a particularly important notion. A sequence is called almost periodic if every factor (finite subword) that appears in it appears infinitely often, and moreover appears with bounded gaps: for each factor there is a bound such that any window of that length in the sequence contains at least one occurrence of the factor. This property captures a strong form of regularity that lies between full periodicity and mere recurrence.

This paper investigates criteria for determining whether morphic sequences are almost periodic. We focus our attention on two natural and widely studied classes of sequences: the fixed points of non-erasing morphisms, and the automatic sequences. In both cases, the central question we address is algorithmic: given a finite description of such a sequence, can we effectively decide whether the sequence it generates is almost periodic?

## Background and Setting

A *morphism* is a mapping from an alphabet to the set of finite words over that alphabet, extended to words by concatenation. A morphism is *non-erasing* if no letter is mapped to the empty word. When a letter is mapped to a word beginning with that same letter, iterating the morphism produces an infinite *fixed point*—a purely morphic sequence. If one additionally applies a coding (a letter-to-letter map) to such a fixed point, one obtains a general *morphic sequence*. The *automatic sequences* form the important special case arising from morphisms of constant length, and admit an equivalent characterization in terms of finite automata reading base-$k$ representations of indices.

These sequences are finitely presentable, which makes them natural candidates for algorithmic analysis. The question of whether a given morphic sequence is almost periodic is thus well-posed as a decision problem, and it is natural to ask about both its decidability and its computational complexity.

## Main Results

The principal contribution of this paper is the development of efficient algorithms for the almost periodicity problem in the two cases mentioned above.

First, for **fixed points of non-erasing morphisms**, we present a polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether the fixed point of a given morphism is almost periodic. The algorithm exploits the self-similar structure induced by the morphism: the way in which factors of the sequence are generated by repeated application of the morphism allows one to reduce the global recurrence question to a finite collection of conditions that can be checked directly on the morphism's description. By analyzing the combinatorial relationships between letters, their images, and the growth behavior of the morphism, we obtain a decision procedure whose running time is bounded by a polynomial in the size of the input.

Second, for **automatic sequences**, we likewise obtain a polynomial-time algorithm. Here the constant-length structure of the underlying morphism—equivalently, the finite-automaton representation—provides additional leverage. The uniform block structure of automatic sequences permits a clean analysis of factor occurrences and their gaps, again reducing almost periodicity to verifiable finite conditions and yielding an efficient algorithm.

## Toward the General Problem

Beyond these two concrete cases, there is a broader open question: is almost periodicity decidable for *arbitrary* morphic sequences, including those obtained by applying a coding to the fixed point of a general (possibly erasing) morphism? It is conjectured that this general problem is decidable. Our final result provides evidence in support of this conjecture. While we do not resolve the general case, the techniques and partial results we establish are consistent with, and lend weight to, the expectation that a decision procedure exists for all morphic sequences. In this way, the polynomial-time algorithms for the two special cases serve not only as results of independent interest but also as stepping stones toward a complete understanding of the decidability landscape for almost periodicity of morphic sequences.

## Conclusion

In summary, this paper establishes that almost periodicity can be decided efficiently—in polynomial time—for fixed points of non-erasing morphisms and for automatic sequences. Together with the supporting result for the general setting, these contributions advance both the theoretical understanding and the algorithmic treatment of uniform recurrence in the class of morphic sequences, and they point toward the eventual resolution of the general decidability conjecture.

# Understanding and Using the Word "Namely"

The word "namely" is a versatile adverb in the English language that serves a specific and useful function: it introduces detailed or precise information about something that was just mentioned. When you want to specify exactly what you mean or provide clarifying examples, "namely" is often the perfect word to bridge a general statement with its specific details.

## What Does "Namely" Mean?

At its core, "namely" means "that is to say" or "specifically." It signals to the reader or listener that you are about to identify precisely who or what you are referring to. For example, in the sentence "Only one student passed the exam, namely Sarah," the word "namely" introduces the specific person being discussed.

## How to Use "Namely" Correctly

"Namely" typically appears in the middle of a sentence, following a general reference and preceding the specific detail. Consider these examples:

- "There is one thing I dislike about winter, **namely** the cold."
- "The company operates in three countries, **namely** France, Germany, and Spain."
- "He excels at several sports, **namely** tennis and swimming."

In each case, the word helps the reader move from a broad idea to concrete specifics without confusion.

## Why "Namely" Is Useful

Using "namely" adds precision and clarity to your writing. Instead of leaving your audience wondering about the specifics, this small word directs their attention exactly where you want it. It is especially helpful in formal writing, academic essays, and professional communication, where accuracy and clarity are highly valued.

## Common Synonyms

If you want variety in your writing, several words and phrases can replace "namely," including "specifically," "that is," "in particular," and "to be precise." However, "namely" remains a favorite because it is concise and elegant.

## Conclusion

Though small, the word "namely" plays an important role in clear communication. By mastering its use, writers can express their ideas with greater precision and guide their readers smoothly from general concepts to specific details.

# Abstract

Morphic sequences, generated by iterating a morphism and applying a coding, constitute a fundamental class of infinite sequences in combinatorics on words, with connections to number theory, dynamical systems, and theoretical computer science. A sequence is *almost periodic* (also known as *uniformly recurrent*) if every factor that occurs in it occurs with bounded gaps. This paper investigates the decidability of determining whether a given morphic sequence is almost periodic.

We present an algorithm that, given a morphism and a coding defining a morphic sequence, decides whether the resulting sequence is almost periodic. Our approach combines structural analysis of the factor graph induced by the morphism with a characterization of recurrence in terms of the reachability and return-word properties of the underlying substitution system. We show that the key obstruction to almost periodicity can be detected by examining the finitely many bounded-length factors and the growth behavior of letters under iteration, distinguishing between bounded, polynomially growing, and exponentially growing symbols.

As a central result, we prove that almost periodicity is decidable for the full class of morphic sequences, resolving the problem uniformly without restricting to purely morphic or primitive cases. We further analyze the computational complexity of the decision procedure and discuss the relationship between almost periodicity, linear recurrence, and minimality of the associated subshift. Several examples illustrate the algorithm and highlight subtleties arising from erasing morphisms and non-primitive substitutions.

Our results extend the known decidability landscape for properties of automatic and morphic sequences, and provide effective tools for reasoning about recurrence in symbolic dynamical systems.

# Abstract

## Uniform Recurrence Criteria for Morphic Sequences

**Abstract.** A sequence is *uniformly recurrent* (or *almost periodic*) if every factor that occurs, occurs with bounded gaps. We investigate decidable criteria characterizing when morphic sequences—those obtained as coding images of fixed points of iterated morphisms—possess this property. For a sequence generated by a non-erasing morphism σ with fixed point *w* = σ^ω(*a*) and a coding τ, we establish that uniform recurrence can be effectively determined by analyzing the structure of the associated Rauzy graphs and the recurrence properties of the underlying letters in the fixed point.

We first treat the case of non-erasing (in particular, primitive) morphisms, showing that primitivity of σ is a sufficient condition for uniform recurrence, while the general non-erasing case requires examining the *bounded* versus *growing* letter dichotomy and the return-word combinatorics of recurrent factors. We provide a complete characterization in terms of the reachability and connectivity properties within the finite automaton describing letter growth.

For the subclass of **automatic sequences**—morphic sequences arising from uniform (constant-length) morphisms—we present a sharpened, algorithmically explicit criterion. Leveraging the finite-state structure of *k*-automatic sequences and the decidability of the first-order logical theory FO(ℕ, +, *V_k*), we demonstrate that uniform recurrence is a decidable property, and we give bounds on the recurrence function in terms of the number of states of the generating automaton.

Our results unify and extend classical theorems (Durand; Allouche–Shallit) on linear recurrence and uniform recurrence, yielding a coherent decision framework spanning primitive, non-erasing, and automatic settings.

**Keywords:** morphic sequences, uniform recurrence, automatic sequences, non-erasing morphisms, symbolic dynamics, decidability.

# Abstract

We investigate the algorithmic and structural properties of almost periodic infinite words, a class that generalizes the classical notion of uniform recurrence while capturing subtler notions of regularity in symbolic dynamics. An infinite word is said to be almost periodic if every factor that occurs at all occurs infinitely often within bounded gaps, a property governed by an associated regulator function. In this paper, we present efficient algorithms for testing almost periodicity and for computing regulators for several important families of infinite words, including automatic sequences, morphic words, and words generated by uniformly recurrent substitution systems.

Our main contributions are twofold. First, we design a decision procedure that, given a finite-state or morphic description of an infinite word, determines whether the word is almost periodic and, when it is, extracts an explicit bound on the recurrence gaps. We analyze the complexity of these procedures and establish tight bounds relating the size of the generating mechanism to the growth of the regulator. Second, we situate these results within a broader logical framework and provide substantial evidence for a general decidability conjecture, which posits that all natural first-order properties of almost periodic words drawn from effectively presented classes are algorithmically decidable.

We support this conjecture by reducing a range of combinatorial questions—concerning factor complexity, appearance functions, and repetition thresholds—to decidable predicates expressible in an extended logical theory of the underlying symbolic system. Our approach unifies previously disparate techniques from automata theory, combinatorics on words, and the model theory of automatic structures. We conclude by discussing the limitations of current methods, identifying obstacles to a full resolution of the conjecture, and outlining directions for extending decidability results to non-automatic almost periodic sequences.

**Keywords:** combinatorics on words, almost periodicity, uniform recurrence, decidability, automatic sequences, morphic words, regulator functions
